title: A lamp for the path
hook: Atisha's short text sets out the stages of the path
carry: has the aim grown its wings

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shantideva's exchange: stand where another stands and look back at yourself. Your line was exchange self and other. Whose hour did you live? Day nine hundred sixty-eight.

A hiker at the edge of a dark trail doesn't need the whole mountain lit up. A small lamp will do, as long as it shows the next few steps and roughly where they lead. We've already met Atisha, the Indian teacher whose coming to Tibet brought a renewal. Tradition says a Tibetan ruler asked him for something simple: not a library, but a guide a person could carry. What Atisha wrote is short. Its title says what it's for. Today: lamrim.
screen: `A SMALL LAMP, A DARK TRAIL.` → `NOT A LIBRARY.` → `A GUIDE YOU CAN CARRY.`

segments.voice: The text is the Lamp for the Path to Awakening. We met its outline when Atisha first came to Tibet. Today, a closer look inside. First, three people. The opening verses sort readers not by school but by aim. Some seek good things for themselves within the round of lives. Some turn from that round toward their own peace. And some want to end the suffering of others as if it were their own. The Lamp says plainly that the rest of it is written for that third person. Second, a wish, then vows. The Lamp asks that person to take refuge and raise the wish to awaken for everyone's sake, the same wish we heard from Shantideva, and then to keep vows. A wish with no conduct behind it stays a wish. Third, the bird. For meditation, Atisha uses a plain picture: a bird whose wings haven't grown can't fly. Without a settled, steady mind, he says, a person can't do much good for others. So calm comes first. Fourth, two wings. Near the end, the Lamp says that wisdom without skillful means is bondage, and skillful means without wisdom is bondage too, so keep both. Insight with no kindness binds; kindness with no insight binds another way. Later Tibetan teachers wrote whole books on this outline, a genre called lamrim, the stages of the path. The Lamp itself is short enough to carry, which was the point. It leaves two questions: what are you aiming at, and has the aim grown its wings?
screen: `THREE PEOPLE, THREE AIMS.` · `A WISH, THEN VOWS.` · `A BIRD WITHOUT WINGS CAN'T FLY.` · `WISDOM AND MEANS, BOTH.` · then, large: `A LAMP FOR THE PATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your own three steps. Settle, and breathe. Ask quietly: what do I want for my own life this year? Let one answer come. Breathe. Then ask: what would real peace look like for me, underneath that? Let one answer come. Breathe. Then ask: what would I wish for the people around me, all of them? Let one answer come. Three steps, in your own words. Then rest in the breath. The bell holds the time.
Lamrim. The stages of the path, the genre Atisha's short text for Tibetan practice gave rise to, sorting the path by aim. Today's word.
Your line: has the aim grown its wings. Today, write your three steps down on paper, in a few words each, and keep them where you'll see them. Day nine hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Atisha's Lamp for the Path to Awakening is studied in Tibetan monasteries and retreat centers, and its outline of three kinds of practitioner shapes the lamrim, the stages-of-the-path teachings given in Tibetan Buddhist communities.

fork.setup: you're Atisha, asked by a Tibetan ruler for help. the teaching in the land is tangled. what do you give him?
options: a vast library of every text from India.
a short guide that lays out the stages by aim.
a list of who is right and who is wrong.
fork.reveal: Atisha wrote a short text, the Lamp, sorting the path into stages by what a person is aiming at.

original.note: Sanskrit for awakening, the first word of the text's Sanskrit title, Bodhipathapradipa: lamp for the path to awakening.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice title for a book.
what it means: a short guide sorting practitioners by aim: small, middle and great.
what a scholar hears: wisdom and skillful means bound together, in an outline later Tibetan teachers expanded into the lamrim.
recall: the Buddha who is to come

sources.ref: Atisha, Bodhipathapradipa (Lamp for the Path to Awakening)

notes: Three kinds of persons (lesser, middling, superior) paraphrased from the opening verses of the Lamp; confirm the paraphrase of each.
The request from a Tibetan ruler (Jangchub Ö of Guge) is given as 'tradition says' and unnamed.
Lamrim as built on the Lamp's outline stated without naming Tsongkhapa or dates; confirm.
Sanskrit title Bodhipathapradīpa and pradīpa 'lamp'; confirm spelling and pronunciation.

Audit: day 936 already taught the Lamp's three aims, 'each stage rests on the one before' and pradipa; the teach, heads, games and original were rewritten to a new angle (written for the great-aim person, vows, the bird with ungrown wings, wisdom and means both bondage alone). Confirm the paraphrases (bird image and wisdom/means verses, approx. vv. 35-43) and bodhi. Review's unsourced 'hardest practice' also cut.
